item.title: JPMorgan sees hedge fund de-risking limiting stock downside, with chips the key gauge
item.description:
The JPMorgan view rests on positioning, so the key test is whether selling dries up even as headlines stay negative. A day of heavy chip losses that is not followed by more forced selling would support the argument. Momentum-driven traders such as commodity trading advisers can flip from sellers to buyers quickly once trends stabilise, which can make rebounds sharp. In credit, CoreWeave’s bonds and default-protection costs are the clearest real-time measure of neocloud funding stress, and any spread into the debt of larger technology issuers would challenge JPMorgan’s view that the problem can be contained. Higher bond yields and oil prices above $110 add a macro headwind, raising financing costs for capital-heavy AI infrastructure at the same time.

---

Earlier:

  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 22 Oct: Nasdaq sinks as AI worries bite; Treasury yields tumble

---

JPMorgan argues the forced selling in chip stocks is largely done, but Thursday’s semiconductor rout immediately put that positioning call to the test.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan strategist Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou says the equity exposure of hedge funds has dropped far enough to suggest limited further downside for stocks.
  • His team found that hedge fund equity performance closely tracks semiconductor shares, and that tight risk limits made recent chip losses worse by forcing funds to cut positions.
  • JPMorgan sees funding concerns around neoclouds as manageable. It notes that neocloud capex of about $80 billion is small against roughly $1.8 trillion of total tech spending this year, and that the tech sector has a financing surplus of about $400 billion.
  • Information technology makes up 28% of the MSCI All Country World Index but takes 40% of hedge fund risk capital. For semiconductors, the figures are 13% and 21%.
  • The note was published Wednesday. On Thursday the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell almost 7%, its biggest daily drop since June, and the Nasdaq lost more than 2.5%.

JPMorgan believes the sell-off in global stocks may be nearing its limit, because hedge funds have already cut much of their equity exposure. However, the bank’s argument faced an immediate test when chip stocks posted their worst session in four months a day after the note was published.

In a flows and liquidity note published on Wednesday and reported by Dow Jones MarketWatch, global markets strategist Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou found a close link between the equity performance of hedge funds and semiconductor shares, as tracked by VanEck’s SMH chip ETF. The two moved closely together during the sector’s rally in the second quarter. When chips began to fall, tight risk limits forced funds to cut positions, which made the decline worse than it would otherwise have been.

The scale of that de-risking is central to JPMorgan’s view. The team believes much of the long positioning in the sector has now been unwound, including by momentum-driven investors such as commodity trading advisers, who account for a large share of daily trading. The strategists acknowledge that short-term headwinds remain, but argue that the positioning adjustment should help limit further losses.

The note also addressed concerns about neoclouds, the specialist providers that rent computing power for AI workloads. Their funding has come under scrutiny after troubles at CoreWeave and a poorly received IPO in South Korea. JPMorgan does not see those problems derailing the AI investment cycle. It argues that demand for computing power is strong enough for providers to pass higher financing costs on to customers. It also notes that neocloud capex of about $80 billion this year is small compared with roughly $1.8 trillion of total tech capex, meaning larger hyperscalers with better access to funding could absorb any shortfall. And it points out that the broader tech sector is generating about $400 billion more in cash flow than it spends on capex this year.

The strongest message in the note is about how much influence chip stocks have. Information technology accounts for 28% of the MSCI All Country World Index by market value, but 40% of the risk capital that hedge funds deploy. For semiconductors, the gap is 13% of index weight against 21% of risk capital. In JPMorgan’s view, that makes chipmakers the best single gauge of global risk appetite, because a move in the sector affects a much larger share of investor capital than its index weight suggests.

That sensitivity was clear on Thursday. The Philadelphia semiconductor index plunged nearly 7%, its biggest daily fall since late June, and the Nasdaq dropped more than 2.5%, its steepest decline since early June, according to Reuters. The trigger was a batch of AI-related earnings that renewed concern about spending. A supply warning from chip equipment maker Lam Research and a CoreWeave downgrade added to the pressure.

Not everyone shares JPMorgan’s calm on neocloud funding. Unsecured debt yields at CoreWeave have climbed to around 15%, a level usually associated with financial distress. HSBC has warned of structural concerns across the neocloud sector, while Goldman Sachs argues that CoreWeave’s reliance on asset-backed financing limits the rise in its borrowing costs.

The next few sessions should show whether Thursday’s slide was a final burst of forced selling or the start of a new leg lower. If the chips trade stabilises without further heavy de-risking, JPMorgan’s positioning call will look well timed. If funding stress spreads beyond the weakest neocloud balance sheets, the cash-flow cushion the bank highlights is likely to be tested. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB’s Panetta says rising yields a drag on growth, not a crisis, ahead of rate meeting
item.description:
Panetta’s remarks put the focus on sovereign spreads, especially French and Italian debt against German Bunds, as the market’s main stress gauge in the euro zone. If US yields keep rising, the spillover he describes could push periphery spreads wider, a risk for Italian bonds given his own warning. For the euro, a growth gap that favours the US alongside higher US yields is a headwind, even with the ECB still facing inflation near double its target. Oil remains the swing factor: sustained high energy prices keep inflation pressure on the ECB, while the drag from tighter financial conditions points the other way. That tension is likely to shape how markets read next week’s decision.

- With policymakers in their pre-meeting quiet period, Panetta’s warning on bond yields is a reminder that markets may already be doing some of the ECB’s tightening for it.

Summary:

  • Bank of Italy Governor Fabio Panetta said the rise in bond yields will weigh on the euro zone economy but is not critical at this stage.
  • He described the bond sell-off as global and led by the US, where growth and inflation have beaten expectations, while European growth is weaker.
  • Panetta pointed to France’s high debt and deficits as a source of pressure, said Germany’s stronger finances have limited its yield rise, and noted spillovers to Italian borrowing costs.
  • Portugal’s central bank governor Alvaro Santos Pereira called for deeper EU integration in services, transport and energy.
  • The ECB is expected to leave rates unchanged at next week’s meeting, and policymakers are in a quiet period on monetary policy.
  • Euro zone inflation is running at almost double the ECB’s 2% target because of surging energy costs.

European Central Bank Governing Council member Fabio Panetta said the recent rise in bond yields will hold back the euro zone economy, though he does not see it as critical for now. His comments come as policymakers prepare for next week’s monetary policy meeting.

Speaking in Turin on Wednesday, the Bank of Italy governor described the move in debt markets as a global phenomenon, driven over the past week by the US, where both growth and inflation have come in stronger than expected. The difficulty for Europe, he said, is that higher US rates come with firmer growth, while expansion in the euro zone is less robust. He described the result as a drag on growth rather than a crisis, according to Bloomberg.

Panetta also pointed to uneven pressure within the bloc. Germany has seen a smaller rise in yields thanks to its stronger public finances, he said, while France’s persistently high debt and budget deficits have kept attention on the bloc’s second-largest economy. He noted that sovereign debt tensions can push up borrowing costs in Italy, and that higher long-term US rates tend to spill over into European markets, including Italian financing costs.

His comments add to warnings from other ECB officials that tighter financial conditions could slow growth. A slowdown could also help contain inflation, which surging energy costs have pushed to almost double the ECB’s 2% target.

Separately on Thursday, Portugal’s central bank governor Alvaro Santos Pereira, also an ECB policymaker, called for renewed momentum behind European integration, Reuters reported. He said Europe’s difficult geopolitical environment and its technological shortcomings show the need to deepen the single market in services, transport and energy. The single market has removed many barriers, he said, but those that remain are harder to fix because they are rooted in national institutions and rules.

Neither official addressed the rate outlook directly, as ECB policymakers are in a one-week quiet period before the meeting, when they cannot comment on monetary policy. Still, the two speeches point to the same problem from different angles: Panetta to the cyclical drag from higher borrowing costs, and Santos Pereira to the structural weaknesses that limit how much growth the euro zone can generate.

That matters for the policy debate. If market-driven increases in yields are already tightening financial conditions, the case for policymakers to add to that tightening themselves becomes harder to make, at least while growth remains fragile. The ECB is widely expected to keep rates unchanged next week. Markets will watch how much weight the statement and press conference give to financial conditions, French fiscal risks and the energy-driven inflation outlook. That balance is likely to shape expectations for the meetings that follow. 

---

The 2026 penultimate European Central Bank meeting is next week:

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 22 Oct: Nasdaq sinks as AI worries bite; Treasury yields tumble
item.description:
• Nasdaq sinks as chip stocks tumble
  • Mag 7 under pressure: Apple bucks the selling
  • Bitcoin follows the flows and today that flow is "risk-off" and selling.
  • The evidence mounts that the US dollar is leveraged to the AI trade
  • US treasury excels $26 billion of five-year tips at a high yield of 2.367%
  • US 10-year yields fall, near 5% level but it's for the wrong reasons
  • Crude oil buyers remain in control from a technical perspective. What would tilt the bias lower?
  • Trading Education: Gold falls despite lower yields: A lesson in trading what the market gives you
  • Canada September PPI +2.0% m/m vs +1.3% prior
  • US initial jobless claims 194K vs 200K estimate. Better than expected.
  • Morning Kickstart: Stocks fall as oil rises on Iran risks
  • investingLive European session wrap: Dollar, yen and bonds kick it old school

U.S. markets traded on two tracks Thursday. Technology and AI-related shares came under renewed pressure, while the Dow and small caps managed modest gains. The Nasdaq lost 2.60%, with the more concentrated Nasdaq 100 falling 2.90%. The Dow’s near-unchanged finish did little to describe the pressure beneath the surface.

The other big move came in Treasuries, where yields plunged by roughly 15–19 basis points. That is a significant decline. Recall the 10 year note reached 5.36% just last week. It is currenly at 4.96%. 

Now, lower borrowing costs would normally give growth stocks some support. Today, that support was missing. Investors remained focused on AI spending and returns, while higher oil kept the inflation problem in the picture.

Dollar mixed; yen leads

The dollar finished mixed. It was strongest against the New Zealand dollar and weakest against the Japanese yen.

USDJPY fell 0.82% to 156.83, while USDCHF declined 0.46% to 0.8206. The sharp drop in Treasury yields helped support those moves. USDCAD also fell, down 0.21% to 1.4015, as higher oil and strong Canadian producer-price data provided a supportive backdrop for the loonie.

Elsewhere, EURUSD declined 0.17% to 1.1213, AUDUSD fell 0.14% to 0.7017, and NZDUSD dropped 0.32% to 0.5682. GBPUSD was little changed, up 0.02% at 1.3397.

The message? Selling in U.S. technology did not produce a broad rush into the dollar.

Treasury yields plunge

The late-session yield snapshot showed:

  • 2-year: 4.6524%, down 17.1 basis points.
  • 5-year: 4.7784%, down 19.2 basis points.
  • 10-year: 4.9612%, down 18.5 basis points.
  • 30-year: 5.2857%, down 15.1 basis points.

The 10-year moved below 5%, with the strongest buying concentrated in the intermediate maturities. That was consistent with investors seeking safety and reassessing the outlook for growth and monetary policy.

During the afternoon, InvestingLive reported that futures pricing assigned a 22% probability to no further Fed hike this year. That still left another increase as the more likely outcome, but traders were giving a pause more consideration. investinglive.com

U.S. stocks: Technology takes the hit

The supplied closing snapshot showed:

  • Dow industrial average: 52,873.28, +11.98 points or +0.02%.
  • S&P 500: 7,663.43, −93.74 points or −1.21%.
  • Nasdaq Composite: 26,008.86, −694.00 points or −2.60%.
  • Russell 2000: 2,784.03, +3.01 points or +0.11%.
  • Nasdaq 100: 28,958.69, −863.83 points or −2.90%.

The gap between the Nasdaq and the Dow was the story. Investors were particularly hard on the technology companies carrying much of the AI investment boom.

Meta fell around 7% during the session, with its spending plans drawing scrutiny. The concern was whether the eventual returns would justify the enormous investment. investinglive.com

My Mag 7 update highlighted Apple (closed up 1.23%) as the exception to the selling across that group. Semiconductor weakness added to the pressure on the Nasdaq indices. The Dow and Russell holding small gains showed that some money was rotating, although the negative breadth meant this was hardly a healthy session underneath. investinglive.com

Overall the Nasdaq composite had it's worst day since June 5th. The Nasdaq 100 had it's worst day since June 23. Both indices closed below their 100 day MAs. 

Economic data: Fewer layoffs, but hiring bears watching

Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 versus 200,000 expected, with the prior week revised to 200,000 from 199,000. The four-week average declined to 197,750. Employers are still holding on to workers.

The offset came from continuing claims, which rose to 1.728 million versus 1.720 million expected. That suggests some workers are taking longer to find another job, although one weekly increase does not establish a trend.

The report offered little evidence of a sharp deterioration in employment. Nevertheless, the subsequent Treasury rally showed that the broader market’s concerns outweighed the stronger initial-claims headline.

In Canada, September producer prices rose 2.0% month over month, following 1.3%, with annual growth accelerating to 14.5%. Raw materials prices jumped 4.8% on the month and 27.0% annually.

Those are pipeline inflation pressures, rather than a direct forecast for consumer prices. Still, they complicate the Bank of Canada’s outlook after the softer CPI report earlier in the week. The supplied morning report put the probability of an October 28 hike near 80%.

Oil rises as Middle East risks persist

Crude oil was trading at $99.07, up $1.92 or approximately 1.98%.

The Middle East continued to provide support. InvestingLive’s coverage highlighted reports of preparations for possible renewed U.S.–Israeli strikes on Iran and intensifying Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Those were reported risks, rather than confirmation that another round of strikes had begun. investinglive.com

As Adam outlined in his post on the Middle East stalemate, the absence of a diplomatic breakthrough continued to hang over energy markets. investinglive.com

That leaves traders facing an uncomfortable combination: falling yields and pressure on growth shares, but oil still near $100. The bond rally does not mean the inflation risk has disappeared. 

Gold and silver fail to find support

Gold was trading at $4,021.61, down $119.41 or 2.88%. Silver fell $3.4024 or 5.87% to $54.5456.

Gold’s decline stood out because Treasury yields were sharply lower. Falling yields normally reduce the opportunity cost of holding a metal that pays no interest. Today, that relationship did not deliver support.

InvestingLive’s gold coverage discussed concerns about tighter financial conditions alongside persistent inflation risks. Position reductions and demand for cash are also plausible explanations for gold falling with equities, although the price action alone cannot establish the cause. investinglive.com

Silver’s larger decline, alongside copper falling 2.68% to $6.4030, was consistent with pressure on industrially sensitive metals as well.

Bitcoin follows the selling

Bitcoin was trading at $81,214, down $2,810 or 3.34%, in the supplied snapshot.

For this session, it followed the pressure in technology and other risk assets. The sharp decline in yields failed to attract enough buying to offset those flows. Bitcoin was offering little protection from the equity selloff.

The next session will test whether technology buyers can regain their footing and whether the Treasury rally signals growing economic concern. Friday’s U.S. flash PMIs provide another growth check, while Middle East headlines remain the wildcard for oil and inflation expectations. Lower yields gave buyers an opportunity today. In technology, gold and Bitcoin, they failed to take it.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump invokes Defense Production Act for oil as pump prices bite 12 days before midterms
item.description:
The memo does little to change the near-term oil balance, which is still driven by the Iran conflict. Brent closed around $113 on Thursday, its highest since early May, after reports that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms. That geopolitical risk premium outweighs any supply response the Defense Production Act can deliver in the coming weeks. The measure is more relevant for refining margins and US refiners: federal financial support for capacity could, over time, ease tight diesel and gasoline cracks that have pushed pump prices above what crude alone implies. Traders are also likely to watch for further pre-election steps aimed at fuel costs, which could add headline volatility to US product futures even if their physical impact is limited.

---

With fuel costs at record seasonal highs and the midterms less than two weeks away, the White House is again using a Korean War-era law to boost oil supply, though any relief at the pump will take longer than the campaign.

Summary:

  • President Trump signed a memo determining that domestic petroleum production, refining and related activities are essential to national defense.
  • The memo invokes Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, which allows federal financial support, purchases and purchase commitments to expand capacity.
  • It builds on an April determination covering petroleum and recent steps, including a Defense Production Act-backed expansion of a Delek refinery in Texas.
  • US gasoline has topped $4 a gallon in October for the first time on record, and diesel has been above $6.
  • Fuel costs have become a central issue before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.
  • Brent crude closed around $113 on Thursday, its highest since May, on reports of planned renewed strikes on Iran.

US President Donald Trump has invoked Section 303 of the Defense Production Act for domestic oil, signing a memo on Thursday that determines petroleum production, refining and related activities are essential to national defense. The move is the White House’s latest attempt to tackle high fuel prices less than two weeks before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.

Section 303 lets the federal government support industrial capacity it considers vital to national defense through purchases, purchase commitments and other financial support. Full details of Thursday’s memo were not immediately available. It follows a similar determination in April covering domestic petroleum production, refining and logistics, which waived some procedural requirements and directed the Department of Energy to use those financial tools to expand capacity.

The administration has stepped up its use of the Korean War-era law in recent weeks. Vice President JD Vance announced at a campaign stop in Texas last week that the Defense Production Act would be used to expand a Delek refinery in Tyler, though neither the White House nor the company detailed the funding or the added capacity. Reuters reported earlier this month that Trump planned to direct department heads to find ways to control diesel prices before the November 3 vote, including by using the law and bypassing state and local rules that restrict energy production. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said the administration is looking to reopen as many refineries as possible.

The political pressure is clear. Gasoline averaged around $3 a gallon when Trump returned to office on a promise to lower the cost of living. Average US gasoline prices have since exceeded $4 a gallon in October for the first time on record, and diesel has traded above $6. The US Energy Information Administration put September’s average retail prices at about $4.35 for gasoline and about $6.30 for diesel, citing higher crude costs and wider refining margins. Heating oil prices in September’s consumer price data were up more than 70% from a year earlier, just as households prepare for winter.

The main driver of those costs remains the war with Iran and disruption to Gulf energy supplies. Brent crude jumped around 4% on Thursday to settle near $113 a barrel, its highest level since early May. The move followed a New York Times report that US and Israeli military planners have prepared for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms. Trump told reporters that the US is not negotiating with Iran and that something would happen fairly soon.

That leaves the administration with limited room to bring prices down quickly. Expanding or restarting refineries takes months or longer, so the Defense Production Act measures address long-term capacity rather than the price voters will see at the pump on election day. The EIA expects retail gasoline prices to stay broadly steady in October before easing slowly in line with crude, a path that depends heavily on how the conflict with Iran develops over the coming weeks.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: OpenAI close to raising up to $30 billion at $1.25 trillion valuation, UAE investors lead
item.description:
The round gives listed markets a fresh read on how private investors are pricing frontier AI after recent volatility in AI-linked shares. A valuation below the roughly $1.4 trillion OpenAI had sought could be read as a sign of greater price discipline. That reading would matter for chipmakers such as Nvidia and for infrastructure names tied to AI capital spending. SoftBank, a major existing OpenAI investor, is among the most direct listed proxies, and its Tokyo-traded shares may respond to any new mark on the stake. The size of Gulf participation also shows how much of the AI buildout depends on sovereign capital, which ties the sector more closely to oil revenues and Middle East geopolitics.

---

Earlier:

  • Nasdaq sinks as chip stocks tumble

---

CNBC (may be gated) report. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round.

The reported valuation is notably lower than the figure OpenAI had been seeking earlier this month. Bloomberg reported in early October that the company was looking to raise at least $30 billion at a pre-money valuation of about $1.4 trillion. According to that report, OpenAI was presenting the valuation to prospective investors as a fixed price, even though it had not yet chosen a lead investor. That approach is unusual for a private round, where investors would normally propose and negotiate terms.

Gulf money has been central to the talks from the start. Bloomberg reported that several UAE funds, including Abu Dhabi-based MGX, were discussing forming a syndicate that could contribute up to $10 billion in total, with BlackRock also in discussions to take part. MGX has backed earlier funding rounds for both OpenAI and Anthropic.

Even at $1.25 trillion, the price would mark a sharp step up from OpenAI’s last raise. The company secured about $120 billion in March at a valuation of about $850 billion, so the new pre-money figure would be nearly 50% higher than seven months ago. Adding $30 billion of new capital would put the post-money valuation at around $1.28 trillion.

Timing appears to be a factor. Reuters reported this week that OpenAI is rushing to secure commitments before Anthropic’s expected stock market listing in mid-November, since both companies draw on a similar pool of investors. Some investors see OpenAI’s push as an attempt to lock in money that might otherwise go to the Anthropic offering, according to the Reuters report. SoftBank, MGX and other existing backers were negotiating to take part. OpenAI has itself pushed back plans for an initial public offering until at least next year.

The company has been making its case to investors with revenue figures. It has told investors that annualised revenue reached about $50 billion following the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, and that it expects to reach $70 billion by the end of the year, Reuters reported. OpenAI has also cut prices on its cheaper models, a move it says has increased usage.

The deal had not been formally announced as of the latest reports, and the terms could still change. Once the round closes, the key questions will be whether the lower valuation reflects investors pushing back on price or a deliberate trade of valuation for speed and certainty, and how much Gulf money will shape the next phase of the AI funding race. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan CPI preview: core seen at 2.1%, topping BoJ target for first time since December
item.description:
USD/JPY has held a tight range this month between just under 157 and just under 159, with the 200-day EMA just above 157.50. A firm print would test the lower end of that range, while a soft one would push the pair back toward 159, where intervention risk becomes the main defence for the yen. In JGBs, the 2-year and 5-year sectors are the most exposed to any repricing of December hike odds, with the 5-year yield near 2.3%. For the Nikkei, a stronger yen and firmer rate expectations would usually hurt exporters and help banks, but AI-linked flows are likely to matter more than the CPI unless the surprise is large. Oil remains the wildcard: sustained crude strength tied to the Middle East conflict keeps energy feeding into Japanese inflation and into the BoJ’s upcoming forecasts.

--- Japan’s core inflation is forecast to clear the BoJ’s 2% target again, which would weaken the case for patience and strengthen the case for a December hike.

Summary:

  • Japan’s national September CPI is due at 2330 GMT Thursday (7:30pm US Eastern), and core inflation (ex fresh food) is expected at 2.1% against 1.7% in August.
  • Headline inflation is seen at around 2.1% from 1.9%, and the ex fresh food and energy measure at around 2.3% from 1.9%.
  • Tokyo’s September data beat forecasts by a wide margin, with core at 2.7% and ex food and energy at 3.0%, pointing to upside risk.
  • The BoJ raised rates to 1.25% in September on a 7-2 vote and is expected to hold at its October 29-30 meeting, with December seen as the next likely move.
  • The 10-year JGB yield has eased to around 2.9% on safe-haven demand, and USD/JPY has held near 158.
  • A September trade deficit about three times the forecast continues to weigh on the yen.

Japan’s nationwide consumer inflation data for September, due at 2330 GMT on Thursday (7:30pm US Eastern), is expected to show core inflation back above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target for the first time since December. That result would strengthen the case for another rate rise before the end of the year.

Core CPI, which excludes fresh food but includes energy, is forecast to have risen 2.1% from a year earlier, according to a Reuters poll of 15 economists, up from 1.7% in August. Economists attribute much of the expected pickup to higher energy costs linked to the Middle East conflict reaching household bills. Other analysts expect headline inflation to rise to around 2.1% from 1.9%. They see the measure that excludes both fresh food and energy, often treated as a gauge of underlying price pressure, at around 2.3%, up from 1.9%.

The risk appears tilted toward a firmer reading. Tokyo’s September figures, released earlier this month, ran well ahead of forecasts: headline and core inflation both reached 2.7%, and the ex food and energy measure hit 3.0%. The Tokyo data are published about three weeks before the national numbers and are widely used as a leading indicator. The comparison is not exact, however. Part of the Tokyo jump came from the expiry of some government support measures, while nationally, electricity subsidies were still holding power prices down in August, when they were about 2.4% lower than a year earlier.

The release comes at a sensitive point for the central bank. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September, its second increase this year. The decision passed on a 7-2 vote, and the two dissenters argued that inflation was still running below target. Core inflation had stayed under 2% for seven consecutive months through August, including through both hikes. A core reading at or above consensus would weaken that objection less than a week before the October 29-30 policy meeting.

Officials have increasingly emphasised upside risks. Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament this week that underlying inflation is very close to the 2% goal. He cited strong global demand linked to artificial intelligence alongside a tight labour market. Deputy Governor Himino has warned of the danger of acting too late. Ueda has also described the bank’s task as anchoring inflation around 2%, rather than trying to lift it as it did during the deflation era.

Even so, an October move is not the base case. Sources familiar with the bank’s thinking told Reuters that the BoJ is likely to keep rates on hold this month unless the yen weakens further and pushes up import costs. The sources said the bank is likely to raise its inflation forecast for next fiscal year as oil prices sustain price pressures for longer than expected, and to keep its focus on inflation risks, leaving room for a hike as soon as December. Market pricing assigns almost no chance to an October increase. Estimates of December odds vary by measure, from around 60% to about 80%.

Japanese government bonds have rallied ahead of the data. The 10-year yield has eased to around 2.9%, its lowest since early September, after peaking above 3.1% in late September. The 30-year yield has fallen to near 3.9%, its lowest since early August. Safe-haven demand linked to the Middle East, fiscal strains in France and volatility in AI-related equities have supported the move. Analysts at MUFG expect the 10-year to trade between 2.85% and 3.00% this week. A firm inflation print would test that rally.

The yen has been stuck. USD/JPY has spent much of October near 158, caught between expectations of further BoJ tightening and steady structural selling of the currency. Japan’s September trade deficit came in at around ¥540 billion, roughly three times the forecast, reflecting the yen that importers must sell to pay their bills. Finance Minister Katayama has not specified an intervention level, but the threat of official buying has helped limit the pair’s upside.

Equities are likely to take their direction mainly from technology. The Nikkei briefly regained the 70,000 mark earlier this month on renewed AI optimism, before a global sell-off in AI and semiconductor shares hit sentiment.

Beyond today’s data, the focus moves to next week’s BoJ quarterly outlook report. In it, the bank is expected to say that underlying inflation has roughly reached 2%, a signal of its readiness to keep raising rates. A national print that confirms the Tokyo signal would support that view. A reading below 2% would revive the dissenters’ argument and leave the yen relying more heavily on the threat of intervention. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq sinks as chip stocks tumble
item.description:
The major U.S. stock indices closed mixed, but the selling in technology shares was the dominant story. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.60%, while the Nasdaq 100 lost 2.90%. The S&P 500 also declined sharply. The Dow and Russell 2000 managed small gains, but neither offered much cushion.

Market breadth was negative. On the Nasdaq, 1,734 stocks declined versus 1,471 advancing. So although the largest losses were concentrated in technology, the weakness extended beyond a handful of heavily weighted names.

Investors continued to question whether earnings and guidance could justify expectations surrounding AI spending. Higher oil prices amid Middle East tensions added another concern. Falling Treasury yields offered little relief to technology shares during the session.

The closing numbers

  • Dow Industrial Average: Up 11.98 points, or 0.02%, at 52,873.28.

  • S&P 500: Down 93.74 points, or 1.21%, at 7,663.43.

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down 694.00 points, or 2.60%, at 26,008.86.

  • Russell 2000: Up 3.01 points, or 0.11%, at 2,784.03.

  • Nasdaq 100: Down 863.83 points, or 2.90%, at 28,958.69.

Chip and AI shares take the biggest hits

Yesterday’s recovery did not provide much protection for buyers today. Semiconductor equipment, chips and AI infrastructure shares were hit particularly hard, with many falling considerably more than the broader Nasdaq indices.

Among the notable technology decliners:

  • Lam Research: Down 11.75% to $230.16.

  • Lumentum: Down 11.54% to $752.54.

  • Astera Labs: Down 11.17% to $257.65.

  • Teradyne: Down 10.63% to $308.75.

item.title: US treasury excels $26 billion of five-year tips at a high yield of 2.367%
item.description:
The Treasury sold $26 billion of 5-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, with the following results:

  • High yield: 2.367%.
  • WI level at the time of the auction: 2.360%.
  • Tail: 0.7 basis point vs the average of 0.2 basis point.
  • Bid to cover: 2.41X vs the average of 2.52X.
  • Directs: 32.4% vs the average of 23.0%.
  • Indirects: 62.1% vs the average of 67.8%.
  • Dealers: 5.5% vs the average of 9.2%.

Auction grade: C−

A somewhat softer auction overall. The Treasury needed to offer a yield 0.7 basis point above the WI level to get the issue sold, a larger tail than average. Bid to cover was also below average, while indirect bidders (foreign buyers) took a smaller share. The offset was strong direct demand (domestic buyers), which helped leave dealers with just 5.5% of the issue—well below average. So there were some positives underneath the headline, but the tail and softer overall bidding keep the grade below a C-.

What are TIPS, and how do they work?

TIPS provide investors with protection against inflation by adjusting the security’s principal with the Consumer Price Index. When inflation rises, the principal increases. The coupon rate stays fixed, but the dollar interest payments increase as that rate is applied to a larger principal balance. Payments are made every six months. www.treasurydirect.gov

For example, take $1,000 of principal with a hypothetical 2% coupon. If the inflation adjustment lifts that principal to $1,030, the annualized interest payment rises from $20 to $20.60. The coupon rate stays the same; the principal used to calculate the payment changes. www.treasurydirect.gov

Today’s 2.367% auction yield is a real yield, meaning a yield above the security’s CPI inflation adjustment. It is separate from the coupon rate and does not represent the market’s inflation forecast. The difference between a conventional Treasury yield and a TIPS yield of the same maturity provides a measure known as breakeven inflation. www.treasurydirect.gov

At maturity, investors receive the inflation-adjusted principal or the original principal, whichever is greater. That floor protects the original face amount, although it does not necessarily protect any premium paid when purchasing the security.

With the current 5 year yield at 4.7909% what does that tell traders/investors?

Using the 5-year Treasury yield of 4.7909% and today’s TIPS auction yield of 2.367%, the spread is:

4.7909% − 2.367% = 2.4239 percentage points, or 242.39 basis points.

That is an approximate 5-year breakeven inflation rate of 2.42%, assuming the yields are measured at the same time and have comparable maturities.

In plain English, the conventional Treasury pays a higher yield because its payments do not adjust for inflation. The TIPS offers a lower real yield, with CPI inflation adjustments added through its principal. The spread represents the inflation compensation priced into the comparison. TIPS Yield Curve and Inflation Compensation

For an investor holding to maturity, roughly speaking:

  • Average CPI inflation above 2.42%: TIPS would tend to deliver the better return.
  • Average CPI inflation below 2.42%: The conventional Treasury would tend to deliver the better return.
  • Average CPI inflation near 2.42%: Returns would be broadly comparable.

That is an approximation; cash-flow timing and reinvestment also matter.

What does today’s auction tell us? The spread is consistent with investors pricing inflation averaging around the mid-2% area over the next five years. It does not mean inflation will be 2.42% every year, or that this is a precise forecast. Breakevens also reflect inflation-risk compensation and differences in liquidity between conventional Treasuries and TIPS. Tips from TIPS: Update and Discussions

The auction itself was somewhat soft, with a 0.7-basis-point tail. Holding the conventional yield unchanged, that higher TIPS yield would narrow the breakeven spread by 0.7 basis point compared with the pre-auction WI level. But that small auction concession alone does not establish that inflation expectations are falling. We would need the earlier spread, using both yields at matching times, to judge the trend.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Meta shares fall 7% on huge spending plans
item.description:
• Q3 revenue $64.6B vs $63.3B expected
  • Q4 revenue guide $73–76B vs $73.7B expected
  • Q3 capex $34.9B; free cash flow turned negative
  • 2026 capex $135–145B (floor raised from $130B)
  • $825B in future spending commitments
  • New nonvoting Class C shares through a 2-for-1 split

Meta beat on revenue, beat on guidance, and the stock is still down 7% and that's a troubling sign for everything touching AI. It's also trading below where it did before the rollout of the impressive Muse app. 

Shares are down intraday to $651.61 and were down 7.3% around midday. Meta was off about 3% premarket at $677.50, and the selling has intensified as the session wears on.

w

The ad business isn’t the problem. Revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, comfortably ahead of estimates. The Q4 range of $73–76 billion has a $74.5 billion midpoint, above the $73.7 billion consensus, and implies roughly 24% growth. Strip out the lawyers and earnings were even better. GAAP EPS was $3.83 vs $3.56 expected and would have been $7.40 without the legal charge.

If you showed me that revenue line a year ago, I’d have said the stock goes up 10%.

The cash flow line

The problem sits below revenue. Q3 capex hit $34.9 billion, up from $31 billion in Q2 and $19.4 billion a year ago. That pushed free cash flow to negative $2.1 billion, the first negative quarter since 2012.

Total expenses rose 68% y/y to $51.6 billion on infrastructure, third-party AI token costs and a $9.9 billion charge tied to an August agreement with several state attorneys general.

Then there’s the number that will stick. A regulatory filing disclosed about $825 billion in future spending commitments for AI data centers, energy and compute, up from nearly $700 billion in July. That includes $356 billion in leases that haven’t started yet and $455 billion in non-cancelable contracts, with $121 billion due in 2027 alone. The two big buckets went from about $139B to $810B in a year, nearly 6x

Class C is the tell

Financing is increasingly a problem throughout the industry. Meta is creating a nonvoting Class C stock, effective January 19, 2027, and distributing it to all holders as a dividend. It works as a two-for-one split.

Meta says the purpose is to give the company the ability to finance its growth and stay ahead of fierce competition at home and abroad. The market is seeing the new class as a currency that will dilute the company.

The obvious comparison is Alphabet’s 2014 recapitalisation. Class C gives Meta stock to use for employee pay, acquisitions and raising capital. With free cash flow negative, buybacks paused and the AI build-out escalating, it lets management issue stock without diluting Zuckerberg’s voting control.

The bears had already done the arithmetic. Oppenheimer projects about $135 billion in AI- and Muse-driven free cash flow losses through 2028, more than Meta’s roughly $90 billion in cash and securities, and it has flagged the risk of an equity raise and now Meta built the tool to do exactly that. The years of buybacks are going to be unwound quickly.

The bull case hasn’t gone away

The sell side isn’t capitulating. Barclays kept its Overweight rating and raised its target to $880 from $780.

Muse adoption is the main argument. Zuckerberg said more than 10 million people in the US and Canada set up Muse personal agents in the first six weeks, and about a quarter use them daily. He used the word non-stop in the call. Meta also said Reality Labs losses should shrink to around $15 billion in 2027 and move toward profitability after that.

The spending is contractual and front-loaded. Revenue from agents is promising but early.

It’s not just Meta

This is bleeding into the broader AI trade. Tech is the weakest sector, led by Nvidia and AMD, and memory makers Micron and SK Hynix are lower too. Lam Research fell as much as 10% after management flagged supply chain constraints into 2027. The Nasdaq is down 2.3%, and the thinking is that there just isn't enough capital out there to build all the AI that hyperscalers want and they're either going to pay more or scale back plans.

That last point matters more than it gets credit for. A company funding an $825 billion build-out is starting to look at equity markets while the risk-free rate is 5%. Every hurdle rate goes up. The patience for “trust us, the ROI is coming” goes down.

The takeaway is simple. Meta’s core business is as strong as it has ever been. But for the first time in more than a decade, it doesn’t generate enough cash to pay for its ambitions, and management just told you how it plans to fill the gap. Until there are hard returns on Muse, the market will price Meta as a capital-hungry AI infrastructure company rather than a cash-printing ad machine. That’s a lower multiple.

At around $1.65 trillion and 22x trailing earnings, Meta looks cheap on earnings. The market is valuing it on cash flow instead.

item.title: Trading Education: Gold falls despite lower yields: A lesson in trading what the market gives you
item.description:
Gold typically benefits when Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar move lower. But “typically” is an important word. Those relationships can help frame an expectation. They do not guarantee the next move.

Why do lower yields tend to support gold? Gold pays no interest. When bond yields fall, investors give up less income by owning gold instead of an interest-paying asset. Falling real yields—yields adjusted for inflation—are particularly supportive.

A weaker dollar can also help. Gold is priced in dollars, so a declining greenback makes it less expensive for buyers using other currencies.

When both move lower, gold can get a double tailwind. However, other forces can outweigh those benefits. A decline in the nominal Treasury yield alone also does not tell us what happened to real yields.

Today provides an educational example.

The U.S. 10-year yield is down around 11 basis points to 5.03%. Just last week, it traded at 5.36%. That is a sharp decline and, taken on its own, would normally be considered supportive for gold.

The dollar’s message is less clear. The greenback is lower against the JPY, CHF and CAD, but higher against the EUR, GBP, AUD and NZD. So the double tailwind is not fully in place.

Nevertheless, with yields falling sharply, traders might reasonably have expected gold to find buyers.

Instead, gold is down around $60 and has traded to its lowest level since August.

That is where the technicals become useful. They give traders a way to assess what the market is actually doing and define where that assessment would need to change.

For me, the technical tools help answer three questions:

  • Bias: Are buyers or sellers more in control?

  • Risk: What level would challenge that view?

  • Targets: If momentum continues, where might the price go next?

The hourly chart shows how that framework has played out.

On October 9, gold moved above its 100- and 200-hour moving averages. That shifted the near-term bias in a more bullish direction. Buyers had their shot, and the price moved higher. However, the rally fell short of the October 2 swing high near $4200.

The subsequent decline initially tried to hold support against the moving averages—the blue and green lines—before breaking below them on October 14. That shifted the bias back toward the sellers.

The price then fell to around $4074, stopping short of the October 7 low at $4066.21 before rebounding.

On October 16, buyers pushed back above the moving averages and got another opportunity to take control. Once again, however, the rally stalled near $4200.

Then came another shift.

On October 19, gold fell below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $4150. It has remained below those moving averages since.

Today’s rebound reached approximately $4146, stalling just short of the 200-hour moving average, currently at $4147.84. Buyers could not get through that technical hurdle, despite the sharp decline in Treasury yields.

The fundamental backdrop offered a reason to look for buying. The price action had yet to confirm it.

With the moving averages holding as resistance, sellers retained control. The subsequent decline broke below the October low at $4066.21 and reached $4057.52.

That puts $4066.21 in focus. After trading below it, can sellers keep the price below the broken floor? Or will the break fail, allowing buyers to recover above it?

Staying below would keep the downside in play, with the next target area between $4000 and $4018. That zone contains swing lows from July and early August, before gold based and rallied toward its August high of $4698.

A sustained break below $4000 would add to the bearish picture and bring another swing area between $3942 and $3959 into view.

On the upside, reclaiming $4066.21 would be an initial step toward stabilizing the price. However, buyers would ultimately need to get back above—and stay above—the 100- and 200-hour moving averages to shift the near-term bias more convincingly in their favor.

Until then, sellers remain more in control.

The lesson is not that the technicals predict every move. The earlier breaks above the moving averages produced rallies that eventually failed. Their value is that they give traders a framework for responding when the market changes.

Today, lower yields offered a potentially bullish influence. Gold’s failure to reclaim its moving averages kept the technical bias bearish, defined a level against which sellers could manage risk, and left lower targets in play.

Traders do not need to resolve every conflicting fundamental signal before making a decision. They do need to know their bias, where that bias would be challenged, and what comes next if the price keeps moving.

Have an expectation. Then make the market confirm it.

item.title: Netflix, Tesla and Meta earnings put Wall Street's cautious mood back in focus
item.description:
Many bulls are somewhat surprised and trapped in today's pre-market

Wall Street may be sending investors an early warning through the way it is reacting to corporate earnings. After Netflix disappointed investors, Meta and Tesla delivered another revealing development: both stocks initially rose following their October 21 earnings announcements, only to surrender those gains and turn negative ahead of Thursday's U.S. trading session.

The concern is not simply that several popular stocks have declined. It is that investors initially welcomed some encouraging results, but that enthusiasm did not last.

For investors holding these companies, or exposed to them through S&P 500 and Nasdaq-linked funds, this changing reaction to earnings deserves attention.

As Justin Low at investingLive.com pointed out, active traders are navigating a fragile tape as U.S. futures tumble amid mounting scrutiny over the AI rally and broader earnings expectations, compounding the bearish tone set by a sharp European market selloff driven by escalating French debt worries and surging bond yields.

This broader weakness in tech sentiment presents a critical headwind for structural mega-deals; as Eamonn Sheridan at investingLive.com recently highlighted, Elon Musk is reportedly rushing to seal a record $3.7 trillion SpaceX-Tesla merger, a transaction heavily reliant on sustaining market enthusiasm as deal currency.

Despite the macro overhang, Eamonn also noted that Tesla's latest earnings call laid out an aggressive target of 5 million vehicles annually by 2030 alongside a sold-out Megapack supply for 2027.

Meanwhile, other tech giants are engineering corporate pivots to maintain investor confidence, with Meta announcing an effective 2-for-1 stock split via non-voting shares to offset a $9.9 billion legal charge, keeping order flow focused on capital allocation as the earnings season rolls on.

Meta and Tesla: When initial optimism turns into selling

Wednesday, October 21, had been a strong session for Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite advanced approximately 1.1%, supported by renewed enthusiasm for technology and AI-related companies.

That made the subsequent earnings reactions particularly interesting.

Meta Platforms (META): From a 4% rally to negative territory

Meta initially jumped more than 4% in after-hours trading following its earnings announcement.

There were legitimate reasons for the early optimism. Third-quarter revenue increased 26% year over year to $64.6 billion, supported by advertising growth and progress in its AI initiatives.

However, investors also had to digest the cost of that growth.

Meta reported negative free cash flow of approximately $2.12 billion for the quarter and projected 2026 capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also announced plans for a new class of non-voting shares to support its investment ambitions.

By Thursday morning, the initial rally had reversed. Meta was down approximately 1.9% in a Reuters premarket update published at 5:40 a.m. Eastern Time.

The question for investors is increasingly whether Meta's AI investments can deliver sufficient future returns to justify their considerable cost.

Tesla (TSLA): A positive earnings reaction that also failed

Tesla offered another example.

Its shares initially gained around 2% after the company released third-quarter results. Positive free cash flow of approximately $1.53 billion, improving gross margins and adjusted earnings that exceeded expectations provided some encouragement.

But that enthusiasm faded as investors evaluated the wider financial picture and management's outlook.

Tesla reduced its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to around $20 billion, compared with its previous expectation of more than $25 billion. The change raised questions about the pace of its ambitious expansion into AI, robotics and autonomous driving.

Tesla shares subsequently reversed lower, falling approximately 5.3% in the same early Thursday premarket Reuters update.

The important observation is the reversal itself.

Investors initially responded positively to aspects of both earnings reports. Later, the market appeared less willing to reward those positives without greater confidence in future profitability and cash generation.

These are premarket observations, not completed Thursday regular-session returns. Nevertheless, they provide a reason to monitor what happens when normal trading resumes.

Netflix had already provided a warning

Earlier in the week, Netflix (NFLX) offered another example of why an earnings beat does not guarantee a positive stock reaction.

Netflix reported third-quarter revenue of approximately $12.87 billion and earnings per share of $0.87, but its outlook disappointed investors.

The company reduced its full-year advertising revenue expectation from approximately $3 billion to $2.7 billion, citing a slower-than-expected rollout of some advertising capabilities.

Its shares subsequently declined.

The three companies face different business challenges. Netflix's concerns relate partly to advertising growth, Tesla's to profitability and investment priorities, and Meta's to the financing and eventual returns from enormous AI spending.

But they share an important characteristic: the market's response was less favorable than some of the reported results might initially have suggested.

That does not mean all three businesses are fundamentally deteriorating. It means investors are becoming more demanding about the relationship between current performance, future expectations and valuations.

Five earnings-season warning signs worth understanding

Investors often concentrate on whether a company beats or misses Wall Street's earnings estimates.

That is useful, but it is only part of the story.

Here are five additional developments that can provide clues about the market's willingness to take risk.

1. Good results, disappointing stock reaction

A company can beat earnings estimates and still experience a substantial share-price decline.

This can happen because investors expected an even better outcome, future guidance disappointed or the stock's valuation already reflected considerable optimism.

The lesson: A company beating expectations is not the same as its stock exceeding investors' expectations.

2. Watch the reaction to the reaction

This is particularly relevant to Meta and Tesla.

The first move following earnings often reflects an immediate interpretation of the headlines. Investors then absorb more detail, including conference-call commentary, expenditure plans and forward guidance.

When an initial rally reverses, it may indicate that buyers are becoming less willing to support the original optimistic interpretation.

However, after-hours trading can involve lower liquidity and sharper price swings. A reversal becomes more meaningful when confirmed during subsequent regular trading sessions.

3. Similar behavior across several major companies

One disappointing earnings reaction could be explained by company-specific problems.

When several influential companies show similar behavior within a short period, the possibility of a broader change in investor sentiment becomes more relevant.

Netflix, Meta and Tesla do not constitute proof of a market-wide problem. They do provide three prominent cases worth comparing with upcoming earnings announcements.

4. Weakness concentrated in the largest stocks

Market capitalization refers to a company's stock market value.

Major indices such as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 are heavily influenced by large companies. A decline in several major constituents can therefore outweigh gains in numerous smaller companies.

This distinction matters for investors holding index funds.

A market may appear relatively balanced when counting how many stocks are rising and falling, yet still suffer meaningful index pressure if the largest companies are doing poorly.

5. Earnings disappointments producing unusually large declines

Options markets can provide an estimate of how far traders expect a stock to move around an earnings announcement.

This is commonly called the implied move. It indicates an anticipated movement range, not a guaranteed limit.

If increasingly large numbers of stocks fall beyond their expected downside ranges, that may suggest a market responding especially harshly to disappointment.

In the provisional October 22 observations underlying this analysis, neither Meta nor Tesla had breached its respective downside expected range. Their significance lies primarily in the failed initial rallies and their influence as major companies, not in exceptionally large individual declines.

Is Wall Street becoming less tolerant of risk?

There is some evidence of increasing selectivity, although it is too early to declare a broader bearish earnings environment.

In the October 13-16 observations considered for this analysis, three of four earnings-reaction sessions showed negative performance when weighted by company size. Downside moves beyond expected ranges also outnumbered upside breaches by 11 to six.

An additional provisional October 22 snapshot showed approximately -2.02% market-capitalization-weighted performance, compared with -0.32% on an equal-weight basis.

Meta and Tesla represented approximately 51.8% of the usable market-capitalization-weighted sample.

These are limited earnings-cohort observations, not returns for the overall stock market, and the sample should not be treated as representative of all reporting companies.

Still, they raise an interesting question: Are earnings-related losses becoming more concentrated in the companies that matter most for the major indices?

There are several possible explanations for the broader unease.

Investors may be reassessing expensive valuations, worrying about the financial burden of AI investment or placing greater emphasis on future cash generation rather than historical earnings beats.

There are also pressures unrelated to individual earnings reports. Rising oil prices, geopolitical uncertainty and broader financial-market volatility weighed on global risk sentiment on Thursday.

It would therefore be a mistake to attribute every price decline solely to a company's results.

What would confirm or weaken the warning?

A single overnight reversal is not sufficient evidence of a sustained market decline.

The next observations are more important than the initial warning.

What would strengthen concerns?

If Meta and Tesla remain weak during regular trading, additional major companies fail to sustain positive earnings reactions, and selling spreads into other sectors, the case for a broader deterioration in sentiment would become more convincing.

Repeated downside moves beyond options-implied expectations would add to those concerns.

What would weaken concerns?

If Meta and Tesla recover their losses, demonstrate sustained buying interest and are joined by positive reactions across a broader range of companies, the initial weakness may prove to have been temporary or company-specific.

Stronger earnings reactions in other industries would be particularly useful evidence that investors remain willing to reward good news.

Investors should distinguish a temporary bout of volatility from a more persistent change in market behavior.

Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon provide the next important test

The next major technology earnings announcements could offer valuable confirmation or contradiction.

Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL/GOOG) are scheduled to report on Wednesday, October 28, while Amazon (AMZN) is scheduled to discuss its third-quarter results on Thursday, October 29.

These companies will give investors additional opportunities to evaluate cloud growth, AI-related expenditures, margins, profitability and management guidance.

The crucial question will not be whether every company beats earnings estimates.

Bulls that bought the initial rally at META right after its after-market-close earnings are especially disappointed and trapped now (if they are still in). Let's look at the 1h chart

Meta's post-earnings rally reverses as sellers take control

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) has experienced a sharp post-earnings reversal. Shares initially surged nearly 8% to just below $749 in after-hours trading, before falling to approximately $676 in premarket trading, almost 10% below that high.

What makes this particularly interesting is the reaction to the initial reaction.

The early rally suggested enthusiasm following earnings, but buyers failed to sustain the advance. Instead, price reversed sharply, breaking below the $705-$711 consolidation area and the pre-earnings closing region around $694-$698.

Two key areas to watch:

  • $673-$675: Immediate support. A sustained break below this area would reinforce the bearish picture, while stabilization could encourage a recovery attempt.

  • $694-$698: The first meaningful recovery test. Reclaiming this area and holding it on a retest would suggest improving buyer interest, with $705-$711 presenting the next obstacle.

The key takeaway is that the reaction after an earnings rally can be more revealing than the initial move. Meta's failed advance suggests that sellers have gained control, at least in the short term.

The next test is whether buyers can defend the recent lows or whether selling pressure continues when regular trading resumes.

NASDAQ: META | One-hour chart | October 22, 2026, premarket snapshot.

It will be whether investors are willing to support positive earnings developments after they have had time to digest the full financial picture.

If encouraging results are repeatedly followed by failed rallies, concerns about investors' appetite for risk would deserve greater attention.

Conversely, sustained positive reactions from these influential companies could suggest that the recent disappointments were selective rather than evidence of a more widespread problem.

The takeaway for stock investors

An earnings report tells us how a business performed relative to expectations.

The subsequent stock reaction tells us something different: whether those results, together with the company's outlook, were enough to justify its existing share price.

The Meta and Tesla reversals make that distinction especially relevant this week.

The market has not established a definitive bearish trend simply because several popular stocks disappointed investors. But the willingness of buyers to defend positive earnings reactions is becoming an increasingly useful development to monitor.

Sometimes the early warning is not the disappointing earnings report. It is the market's inability to hold a rally when the news initially looked encouraging.

item.description:
• Prior was +1.3% m/m
  • PPI y/y 14.5% vs 13.5% prior
  • Raw materials price index 4.8% m/m vs 3.3% prior
  • Raw materials price index 27.0% y/y vs 22.9% prior

The market is pricing in an 80% chance of a Bank of Canada rate hike on October 28. This week's CPI number was on the low side but this data point highlights the inflation in the pipeline.

USD/CAD is down 10 pips to 1.4035 today and that highlights how the dynamic in the FX market has totally flipped. S&P 500 futures are down 0.9% but the market sees it as money fleeing the US AI trade, not a traditional 'risk off'.

For background, Canada’s producer price data come in two monthly reports from Statistics Canada: the Industrial Product Price Index (IPPI) and the Raw Materials Price Index (RMPI). They’re typically released together at 8:30 am ET, a few weeks after the reference month ends.

The IPPI measures prices that Canadian manufacturers receive for goods as they leave the factory gate, covering everything from refined petroleum and lumber to metals, chemicals, food products and motor vehicles. The RMPI tracks the prices manufacturers pay for raw materials, including crude oil, metal ores, logs, grains and livestock. Many of those inputs aren’t produced in Canada, so the RMPI is effectively a gauge of global commodity costs flowing into Canadian industry.

The headline figures are the monthly and annual changes in each index, and neither is seasonally adjusted. Because energy dominates, StatCan also publishes the IPPI excluding energy and petroleum products, which gives a cleaner read on broader factory-gate pricing.

The Canadian dollar is a big driver. Many Canadian exports, such as lumber, metals and energy, are priced in US dollars, so a weaker loonie raises the Canadian-dollar value of those goods and lifts the IPPI. A stronger loonie does the opposite. Some swings in the index reflect currency moves rather than any change in underlying pricing pressure.

Unlike the US PPI, the Canadian reports cover only goods and don’t feed into a preferred inflation gauge, so they rarely move markets. They’re mainly watched as an early signal of cost pressures that could eventually reach consumer prices, and of how commodity swings and tariffs are hitting Canadian producers’ margins.

  • Initial claims four-week average: 197,750, down 1,000. Prior revised to 198,750 from 198,500.

  • Continuing claims four-week average: 1,711,000, up 4,000. Prior revised to 1,707,000 from 1,708,750.

  • Insured unemployment rate: 1.1%, unchanged.

US initial jobless claims fell to 194,000, according to the Department of Labor’s weekly report. The decline reverses the previous week’s increase, while the four-week average moved lower as well. Both point to employers continuing to hold on to workers.

The offset came from continuing claims, which increased 25,000 to 1.728 million. That suggests some difficulty finding another job among workers receiving benefits, although one weekly increase does not establish a trend.

Before seasonal adjustment, initial claims fell 19,321, a larger decline than the 14,179 anticipated by seasonal factors. Unadjusted initial and continuing claims also remained below their comparable year-earlier levels.

Quick analysis: Fewer new claims are encouraging, but the hiring side still bears watching. This report gives the Fed little evidence of a sharp deterioration in employment. In isolation, the lower initial reading could support the dollar and Treasury yields by reducing the urgency for rate cuts. The increase in continuing claims tempers that signal. The question now is whether that increase persists.

What this report measures: Initial claims count new applications for unemployment insurance and provide a timely indication of layoffs. Continuing claims track ongoing benefit claims and can help show how quickly unemployed workers are finding jobs. The headline figures are seasonally adjusted, subject to revision, and cover different weeks, with continuing claims lagging initial claims by one week.

  • Brent crude up 2.8% to $111.88
  • 10-year Treasury yields down 9 bps to 5.05%
  • Gold up 2.0% to $4,060
  • European equities tumble; S&P 500 futures down 1.0%
  • Bitcoin down 3.4% to $81,738

It's been a while since we've reverted back to the classic risk-off move in markets, but this is about as close as it gets.

As geopolitical tensions linger and equities are being sent to the cleaners, we're seeing a return of old school risk-off flows in markets. The dollar and yen are bid among major currencies while bonds are also trading higher i.e. yields lower. The only notable difference is in commodities as oil is up and gold is down instead.

US-Iran tensions are still messing around with the risk mood, keeping oil markets on edge and that is seeing Brent crude push above $111 to its highest since May. And as inflation fears return, that is causing tech stocks to tumble lower alongside concerns over the AI rally as investors start to question whether the massive spending can produce the necessary results to support the already lofty valuations.

S&P 500 futures are down 1.0% while Nasdaq futures are down 1.7%. And over in Europe, French fiscal risks continue to weigh on the overall mood with the France-Germany 10-year yield spread breaking out to 170 bps - its highest since 2011. That is seeing stocks erase the gains from yesterday with the DAX falling by 0.8% and CAC 40 down by 1.2%.

In the major currencies space, it's one of those classic days where the dollar, yen, and franc are all bid against the rest of the bloc. USD/JPY is down 0.7% to 157.05 while EUR/USD has tumbled from 1.1240 to 1.1195 during the session, as the euro struggles amid growing fiscal worries in France. EUR/CHF itself is also falling to a three-month low in testing the 0.9200 level.

Besides that, gold is weighed down after weeks of consolidation in a drop below $4,100 today. That is leading to further selling pressures as the precious metal is unable to catch a break in falling to $4,060 on the day. And that is despite Treasury yields also dropping hard, with 10-year yields easing lower to 5.05% as investors look to be favouring growth concerns once again.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: The Japanese yen is once again acting as a safe haven as growth concerns replace inflation fears
item.description:
USD:

The US dollar has recently been driven mainly by growth concerns rather than inflation fears. In fact, despite hotter US inflation data last week, Treasury yields dropped significantly and rate hike probabilities saw a slightly dovish repricing. Given the overstretched long positioning in the greenback, we’ve started to see an unwind which could extend further if growth concerns strengthen.

That’s why tomorrow’s US Flash PMIs could be an important catalyst. Strong data could quell those fears and give the US dollar a boost. A soft report, on the other hand, will likely increase growth concerns and put further pressure on long-term Treasury yields and the greenback.

JPY:

On the JPY side, the currency has started to act like a safe haven as market’s focus shifted to growth. The changes in risk sentiment have been responsible for the daily ebb and flow as BoJ interest rate expectations remained largely unchanged.

The BoJ is expected to hike by 25 bps in December and deliver two more rate hikes in 2027. If global growth deteriorates, though, the central bank might find itself once again hiking into a slowdown. 

For background, the BoJ has often been criticised for tightening too late because deflation fears have always clouded the central bank’s judgement. This time may not be so different, but the JPY would still be supported in case of a global slowdown due to extreme bearish positioning and safe haven flows.

 

USDJPY TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that USDJPYis consolidating between the 155.00 support and the 160.50 resistance. There’s not much we can glean from this timeframe, as the buyers will have a better risk to reward setup around the support, while the sellers will look for short opportunities around the resistance.

USDJPY TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we can see the price is rejecting the minor support zone around the 156.60 level. We can expect the buyers to step in here, with a defined risk below the support, to position for a rally into the 160.50 resistance. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to pile in for a drop into the 155.00 support next.

USDJPY TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as from a risk management perspective, the buyers will have a better risk to reward setup around the support, while the sellers will need a break to open the door for new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Today, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures, while tomorrow we conclude the week with the Japanese CPI report and the US Flash PMIs. The developments in the Middle East, though, will remain in focus.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.
